title: Quiz League Final Cutoff
aka: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
story: A pub quiz league sends its best k teams to a grand final. Teams finish their seasons on different nights, and each season total is posted once final. Wrong answers cost a point, so a total can be negative.
The league website shows the cutoff, which is the total a team currently needs to be in the top k. The cutoff must update as soon as each new total arrives.
task:
• constructor(k, totals) receives k, the number of final places, and totals, the list of totals already posted, which may be empty.
  • add(total) records one more posted total and then returns the k-th highest total posted so far. If fewer than k totals have been posted, it returns null (None in Python).
Equal totals take separate places: if the top totals are 50, 50 and 40, the 2nd highest is 50 and the 3rd is 40.

examples.explanation: The top 3 starts as 42, 30 and 17. Adding 25 pushes out 17, so the cutoff is 25. Adding 50 pushes out 25, so the cutoff is 30. Adding 10 is too low to enter the top 3, so the cutoff stays 30. Adding 42 pushes out 30, so the top 3 is 50, 42 and 42, and the cutoff is 42.
With one total there is no 2nd place yet, so the result is null. After 8 is added, the top 2 is 8 and -5, so the cutoff is -5. Then 3 pushes -5 out, so the cutoff becomes 3.

hints: In the first example, once the top 3 is 42, 30, 25, a total of 10 arrives. Can a total below the current cutoff ever matter again?
A total that falls out of the top k never comes back, because new totals only push the cutoff up. So you only need to keep k totals.
The answer is the smallest of the k totals you keep. Each new total is compared with it and may replace it. Which data structure gives you the smallest item and lets you replace it in O(log k)?

Keep a min-heap of at most k totals. To add a total, push it, and if the heap now holds more than k items, pop the smallest. If the heap holds exactly k items, its top is the answer, and otherwise return null. Load the starting totals the same way.
bruteForce: The brute force keeps every total in a list. On each add it appends the total, sorts the list from high to low, and reads position k - 1.

Each call costs O(n log n) for n totals so far. With 10,000 starting totals and 10,000 calls, each sort handles between 10,000 and 20,000 totals, which is about 2 billion steps for the season. Inserting into a sorted list is better, but shifting the elements still costs O(n) per call.

walkthrough: You only need the current top k totals, and among those the weakest one, because it is the cutoff and the first to be pushed out. A min-heap of size k keeps that total on top.
• The constructor pushes 42, 17 and 30. The heap holds 17, 30 and 42, with 17 on top.
• add(25) pushes 25, so the heap has 4 items, and then pops the smallest, 17. The heap holds 25, 30 and 42, and the call returns 25.
• add(50) pushes 50 and pops 25. The heap holds 30, 42 and 50, and the call returns 30.
• add(10) pushes 10 and immediately pops it again, so the heap is unchanged and the call returns 30.
• add(42) pushes 42 and pops 30. The heap holds 42, 42 and 50, and the call returns 42.
To track the highest totals you use a min-heap, because a max-heap would put the highest total on top, and that is the one total you never need to look at.
solution.timeWhy: Each add does one push and at most one pop on a heap that never holds more than k + 1 items. The constructor costs O(n log k) for n starting totals.
solution.spaceWhy: Only the top k totals are kept.
solution.takeaway: To find the k-th largest value so far in a stream, keep a min-heap of size k. Its top is the answer, and anything smaller than the top can be discarded for good. For the k-th smallest, use a max-heap of size k instead.
